title: How to Share Your Faith Without Being Weird
excerpt: Most of us are either silent or strange. There is a third way, and it looks more like Jesus than either of the first two.
body:
Most Christians live between two failures. The first is silence. We never say a word about the most important thing in our lives because we are afraid of the awkwardness, and we tell ourselves we are being respectful when we are mostly being scared. The second is strangeness. We finally work up the nerve and then we ambush a coworker in the break room with a script that has nothing to do with the conversation we were actually having. Both failures come from the same place. We have made evangelism a performance instead of a relationship.

The weirdness is not the gospel. The weirdness is us.

## Why we get strange

We get strange when we treat people as projects. A project has a deadline, a deliverable, and a close. When you walk into a coffee shop and the person across from you is a target rather than a neighbor, they can feel it. You are not listening. You are loading. You are waiting for the gap in the conversation where you can insert the thing you came to say. People are not stupid. They know when they are being worked.

Jesus did not work people. He ate with them. He asked them questions he already knew the answers to so they could discover something true about themselves. He let the woman at the well change the subject five times before he told her who he was. He was unhurried because he was not trying to close. He was trying to love.

## Start with the conversation you are already in

The single most useful shift is this: stop trying to start a spiritual conversation and start paying attention to the one already happening. People tell you what is breaking their hearts if you are quiet long enough to hear it. A marriage straining. A parent slipping into dementia. A kid who will not speak to them. A job that pays well and means nothing. These are not detours from the spiritual conversation. They are the spiritual conversation. You do not have to import the gospel from somewhere else. You have to recognize that it is already relevant to the thing this person just told you.

When a friend says they are exhausted, you do not need a tract. You need to ask what is underneath the exhaustion. That question is more evangelistic than most sermons because it tells the person they are worth your attention.

## Say less than you think you need to

The instinct, once you finally speak, is to say everything at once. Resist it. You are not responsible for converting anyone. You are responsible for being honest about what you have found. "I don't know how I would have gotten through that year without my faith" is a sentence. It is true, it is short, and it opens a door without shoving anyone through it. Then stop talking. Let them ask. If they do not ask, you have still told the truth, and the truth does not expire.

Peter tells the scattered church to always be ready to give a reason for the hope in them, and then he adds a phrase we skip over: with gentleness and respect. The readiness and the gentleness are not in tension. The gentleness is what makes the readiness believable.

## Let your life be the strange part

The early church grew in a hostile empire not mainly through arguments but through a way of living that did not make sense to the people around them. They took in abandoned babies. They stayed in the city during the plague when everyone with means fled. They forgave. The strangeness that draws people is not awkward conversation. It is a life that cannot be explained by the ordinary motives of self-protection and self-advancement.

I have to confess that for years my evangelism was loud and my life was unremarkable, which is exactly backward. The people who pulled me toward faith were not the ones who cornered me. They were the ones whose patience I could not account for.

## When you do say it plainly

There are moments to be direct, and you will know them. Someone asks you straight out what you believe. Someone in crisis asks if God could possibly want them. In those moments, do not hedge. Tell them about Jesus simply and without apology. Directness is not weirdness. Weirdness is forcing directness where the conversation has not asked for it.

The Great Commission tells us to make disciples, and a disciple is a learner walking with a teacher over time. That is the shape of it. Not a transaction. A walk.

## This week

Pick one person you see regularly and decide you will ask them a real question and then listen without steering. Not to set up a pitch. Just to learn what is actually heavy for them. Pay attention to whether you are loading while they talk. If you catch yourself loading, set it down and keep listening. That habit, repeated, will do more than any script you could memorize.
